title: Pluckley: Inside the UK Village known for its ghostly legends, haunted corners and spine-chilling supernatural sightings
byline: TOI Lifestyle Desk / etimes.in / Nov 09, 2026, 04:00 IST
content:
Image Courtesy: WikiMedia Commons

Are ghosts real?This English village certainly proves so.There is no place better for picturesque and lush green landscapes, for days in quaint countryside, than the United Kingdom.

Its small towns and villages transport you to scenic beauties we only see on our laptop screensavers.But, one such village hides more than small-town secrets. In fact, its secrets are wide open, given it being mentioned in the Guinness Book World Record.This is the story of Pluckley, a village and civil parish in the Ashford district of Kent, England.Details about Pluckley

Image Courtesy: WikiMedia Commons

Pluckley sits on the northern edge of the Kentish Weald, between Maidstone and Ashford.

It is a long-established settlement, with roots going back to Anglo-Saxon times. The village appears in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Pluchelei, and its name is believed to come from the Old English words for 'Plucca's clearing'.Stepping in the town makes you want to put your phone away and take a walk amongst the orchards, sheep grazing in open fields, old houses and green lanes. At its centre stands St Nicholas' Church, whose oldest sections date back to the medieval period.

The town, on last count in 2021, has 1083 residents, not including the 12 “official” ghosts. Yes, ghosts can be official and unofficial, at least in Pluckley.It has been featured in much of pop culture and media, whether making it a setting for the 1990s series The Darling Buds of May, based on H. E. Bates' novels; or investigations into its haunted reputation.Pluckley is often called England's most haunted village, with the number of reported spirits varying between 10 and 17.

It received a mention in the 1989 Guinness Book of World Records under the haunted villagse category.

Ghosts of Pluckley

Image Courtesy: WikiMedia Commons

One of the most famous ghoul is the Red Lady, believed to be a member of the Dering family. She is said to wander around St Nicholas' Churchyard, searching for the grave of her stillborn child. Another is the White Lady, supposedly buried in seven coffins and an oak sarcophagus. Her spirit is said to haunt the church and its grounds.Then there is the Watercress Woman, a seller who is believed to have caught fire while smoking a pipe near a bridge. The story says that her ghost appears wrapped in flames, crying for help. This is similar to the 1911 incident when a watercress seller named Sarah Sharp died after her clothing accidentally caught fire, possibly from her smouldering tobacco pipe.The Screaming Man of the Clay Pit is another familiar name. His ghost is said to scream after a worker was buried under a collapsing wall of clay at the village brickworks; matching records of a man named Richard Bridgland who died in an accident there in 1899.The Hanging Schoolmaster is said to haunt Dicky Buss's Lane, while a highwayman reportedly appears near the hollow tree where he was killed. Other stories include a colonel who hanged himself in Park Wood, a woman who died by suicide at Rose Court, a phantom coach and horses, and a monk said to haunt Greystones. Dering Woods, meanwhile, is better known by its more unsettling nickname, the Screaming Woods, thanks to stories of disembodied cries heard at night.However, the stories were not all passed down unchanged. A 2025 study by Dr Simon Moreton of the University of the West of England traced many of them to the writings of local historian and ghost-hunter Frederick Sanders. Sanders first called Pluckley 'the most haunted village in England' in a 1950 newspaper article, listing ten ghosts. His accounts were drawn from local stories and real incidents, although he sometimes embellished details or mixed up people and events.The supposed schoolmaster, for instance, was actually a papermaker named Henry Edgar Martin.

Three other stories, including the phantom coach and horses, the monk of Greystones and a poltergeist at Surrenden Dering, were later fabricated by actor and radio presenter Desmond Carrington for a 1962 magazine article. As the stories appeared in books and newspapers, the village's ghost count grew.The stories have since attracted curious visitors, particularly around Halloween. However, not everyone in the village welcomes the crowds.

Some residents have raised concerns about visitors disturbing the churchyard and leaving behind rubbish and fires.A trip to Pluckley might leave you with more questions than answers, especially if you happen to hear a scream in the woods or spot a figure wandering around the churchyard. With centuries-old stories, the village certainly has no shortage of company after dark. And really, who needs a quiet countryside getaway when you can have a little paranormal activity on the side?
